lessons.title: Manual Peeling vs. Mechanical Peeling
lessons.body: Peeling removes the outer brown skin and the inner pinkish layer (cortex) of cassava roots. Manual peeling uses a sharp knife or machete. Hold the root firmly, cut off the ends, then slice lengthwise through the skin and peel it back. For 100 kg of roots, one person can peel about 20-30 kg per hour. Mechanical peelers are machines with abrasive drums or blades that rub off the skin. They can process 500-1000 kg per hour but cost $500-$3000. In Africa, manual peeling is common for small-scale operations because it is cheap and creates jobs. However, mechanical peeling is faster and reduces labour costs for large processors. When choosing, consider your daily root volume. If you process less than 500 kg per day, manual peeling is better. If more, a mechanical peeler pays off within months. Also, mechanical peelers may remove too much flesh, leading to starch loss. Manual peeling allows you to control depth. For starch extraction, you want to remove all skin and cortex because they contain bitter compounds and dirt. After peeling, roots should be processed within 24 hours to avoid spoilage. Always use clean, sharp knives to avoid bruising. Train peelers to remove only the skin and thin cortex, leaving the white flesh intact. In many African villages, groups of women peel together, sharing tips and increasing speed. You can also use a simple hand-cranked peeler made from a metal drum with rough interior. This costs less than $100 and speeds up peeling. Remember, the goal is clean, white roots ready for washing. Peeling is the first step to high-quality starch.

lessons.title: Washing and Sanitizing Roots
lessons.body: After peeling, cassava roots carry dirt, sand, and microbes. Washing removes these to prevent starch contamination. You need three basins or drums: first for rough washing, second for rinsing, third for sanitizing. Use clean water. For 100 kg of roots, use about 200 litres of water. In the first basin, add 1 tablespoon of salt per 10 litres to help remove dirt. Scrub roots with a soft brush or hands. Change water when it becomes muddy. In the second basin, rinse with clean water. In the third basin, add 1 tablespoon of bleach (sodium hypochlorite) per 10 litres of water. Soak roots for 5 minutes. Bleach kills bacteria and mould. Do not use too much bleach; it can affect starch quality. After sanitizing, rinse again with clean water. If you don't have bleach, use lemon juice or vinegar (1 cup per 10 litres) as a natural sanitizer. In rural Africa, many use river water, but it must be filtered or boiled first. Boiling kills microbes but takes fuel. Solar disinfection (putting water in clear bottles in sun for 6 hours) is a cheap alternative. After washing, roots should be white and free of smell. Wet roots are slippery, so handle carefully. Use a clean surface to drain. Do not let roots sit in dirty water; they absorb contaminants. For small operations, wash in a large plastic tub. For larger, build a concrete washing bay with sloped floor and drain. Always wash your hands and tools before starting. Clean water is key to safe starch. If you skip sanitizing, starch may ferment or smell bad. In markets, buyers pay more for clean, white starch. So invest time in washing.

lessons.title: Cutting and Slicing Roots for Grating
lessons.body: Whole cassava roots are too large for most graters. You must cut them into smaller pieces, usually 5-10 cm long and 2-3 cm thick. Use a sharp knife or machete on a clean wooden board. Cut roots crosswise into chunks, then slice lengthwise if needed. The size depends on your grater: manual graters need smaller pieces (2-3 cm), while motorized graters can take larger chunks (5-8 cm). For 100 kg of roots, cutting takes about 30-45 minutes with two people. Wear gloves to avoid cuts and skin irritation from cassava juice. Cut on a stable surface; never hold root in your hand while cutting. A common method is to split the root lengthwise into quarters, then cut into short lengths. Remove any woody core or fibrous parts. These can clog the grater. Also remove any dark spots or rotten areas. After cutting, pieces should be uniform for even grating. If pieces are too big, the grater may jam or produce coarse pulp. If too small, you waste time and get fine mush that is hard to press. In Africa, many use a simple wooden block with a knife attached, called a 'cassava cutter'. You can also use a mechanical chopper, but it costs more. For small scale, hand cutting is fine. Keep your knife sharp; a dull knife bruises the root and releases more water. Cut roots just before grating to prevent browning. If you must wait, soak pieces in clean water with a little salt (1 teaspoon per litre) to prevent discoloration. After cutting, proceed immediately to grating. Do not let cut pieces sit for more than 30 minutes. This step is simple but critical for efficient grating and high starch yield.

lessons.title: Removing Foreign Materials and Defects
lessons.body: Cassava roots can contain stones, sand, pieces of wood, and damaged parts. These must be removed before grating. Foreign materials damage graters and lower starch quality. After washing, inspect each root. Look for dark spots, soft areas, or holes from insects. Cut these out with a knife. Also remove any roots that are completely rotten or mouldy. They contain toxins that can spoil the whole batch. For 100 kg, expect to discard 5-10 kg of defective roots. Use a clean table or mat to spread roots. Work in good light. A simple method is to float roots in water: healthy roots sink, while some foreign materials float. But stones sink too, so also use your hands. For small stones, a mesh screen (1 cm holes) can help. Place roots on screen and shake; sand and small stones fall through. For larger operations, use a destoner machine, but it is expensive. Manual removal is fine for up to 1 tonne per day. Also check for metal pieces, glass, or plastic from packaging. These can break your grater. Train workers to be vigilant. Keep a bucket for waste. After removing defects, cut roots into pieces as described in Lesson 3. Inspect again after cutting; sometimes defects are hidden inside. Remove any brown or black streaks. The presence of foreign materials can cause off-flavours and may even damage equipment. In many African markets, starch with dark specks sells for less. So take time to clean. Use clean water to rinse roots after trimming. Change water frequently. A simple magnet can remove iron particles if you suspect them. For quality starch, this step is non-negotiable. It takes about 15-20 minutes per 100 kg. Do it well, and your grater will last longer and your starch will be purer.

lessons.title: Size Reduction: Grating and Rasping
lessons.body: Grating breaks cassava root cells to release starch granules. You can use a manual grater (a metal sheet with punched holes) or a motorized rasping machine. Manual grating: hold a piece of root and rub it against the rough surface. It takes about 1 hour to grate 10 kg. Motorized graters use a spinning drum with sharp teeth. They can process 500-1000 kg per hour. In Africa, many small processors use a locally made motorized grater powered by a 5-10 HP diesel engine or electric motor. The cost is $300-$1000. For manual grating, the root must be cut small (2-3 cm). For motorized, pieces can be larger (5-8 cm). The goal is to produce a fine pulp, not chunks. The finer the pulp, the more starch you extract. After grating, the pulp should be a smooth, wet mash. If it is too coarse, starch remains trapped in cells. You can run the pulp through the grater twice. Add a little water during grating to prevent overheating and to help starch release. For motorized graters, adjust the gap between the drum and the casing. Too tight causes jamming; too loose gives coarse pulp. Test with a handful of roots. In many villages, people use a 'cassava grater' made from a car wheel with nails hammered through, mounted on a frame. This works but is slow. A better option is a hammer mill with a screen, but it may bruise the starch. The best is a dedicated rasping machine with stainless steel teeth. After grating, the pulp is ready for pressing or settling. Work quickly; grated pulp darkens if left in air. Add 1 litre of water per 10 kg of pulp to keep it wet. If you are using a manual grater, take breaks to avoid blisters. Wear gloves. This step is the heart of starch extraction. A good grater can increase yield by 20%. So invest in a quality grater or maintain your manual one well.

lessons.title: Maintaining Equipment for Grating
lessons.body: Grating equipment must be cleaned and maintained daily. After use, rinse the grater with clean water to remove cassava pulp. Leftover pulp hardens and can break teeth or clog holes. For manual graters, use a stiff brush to scrub the rough surface. For motorized graters, open the casing and remove all pulp. Use a wooden scraper, not metal, to avoid damaging the drum. Wash with water and a little detergent. Rinse well. Dry with a cloth. Every week, check the teeth or blades for wear. Dull teeth produce coarse pulp and reduce starch yield. Sharpen or replace them. For a manual grater, you can sharpen the punched holes with a file. For motorized, replace the drum or teeth as recommended by the manufacturer. Lubricate bearings and moving parts with grease or oil every 50 hours of use. Check belts and tighten if loose. A loose belt slips and reduces grating speed. Also check the motor: clean air filters, change oil every 200 hours. In dusty African environments, clean the motor weekly. Store equipment in a dry place, covered with a tarpaulin. Rust is a major enemy. If you use a mild steel grater, coat it with cooking oil after drying. Stainless steel is better but more expensive. For manual graters, hang them on a wall. For motorized, keep in a shed. Train one person to be responsible for maintenance. Keep a logbook: date, hours used, maintenance done. Replace worn parts before they break. A broken grater stops production. In many projects, equipment fails because of neglect. Simple daily cleaning adds years to life. Also, ensure the power source is stable. If using a diesel engine, check fuel and oil daily. For electric, use a voltage stabilizer. With good care, a motorized grater can last 5-10 years. Manual graters can last 2-3 years if cleaned and sharpened. Remember, maintenance costs less than replacement. So make it a habit.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of manual peeling over mechanical peeling for small-scale cassava processors?
options: B) It is cheaper and creates jobs
quiz.explanation: Manual peeling is low-cost and labour-intensive, providing employment in small operations.

quiz.q: Approximately how many kilograms of cassava can one person peel manually per hour?
quiz.explanation: A skilled person can peel about 20-30 kg of roots per hour manually.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid removing too much flesh during peeling?
quiz.explanation: Removing excess flesh reduces the amount of starch available for extraction.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding salt to the first washing basin?
quiz.explanation: Salt helps loosen dirt and makes scrubbing more effective.

quiz.q: How long should roots be soaked in a bleach solution for sanitizing?
quiz.explanation: A 5-minute soak in diluted bleach kills most bacteria and moulds.

quiz.q: What is a cheap alternative to bleach for sanitizing cassava roots?
quiz.explanation: Lemon juice or vinegar are natural sanitizers that can be used if bleach is unavailable.

quiz.q: Why should cut cassava pieces be uniform in size before grating?
options: A) For even grating and better starch yield
quiz.explanation: Uniform pieces ensure consistent grating and prevent clogging or coarse pulp.

quiz.q: What should you do to prevent cut cassava pieces from browning if you must wait?
quiz.explanation: Soaking in salt water slows enzymatic browning.

quiz.q: What is a common tool used for cutting cassava roots in Africa?
options: B) A sharp knife or machete
quiz.explanation: A sharp knife or machete is the standard tool for cutting roots.

quiz.q: Why is it important to remove foreign materials like stones before grating?
options: B) They damage graters and lower starch quality
quiz.explanation: Stones and other foreign objects can break grater teeth and contaminate starch.

quiz.q: What percentage of roots might be discarded as defective during inspection?
quiz.explanation: Typically 5-10% of roots are discarded due to rot, insects, or damage.

quiz.q: Which method can help remove small stones from cassava roots?
quiz.explanation: A mesh screen allows sand and small stones to fall through while roots remain.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of grating cassava roots?
options: B) To break cells and release starch granules
quiz.explanation: Grating ruptures cell walls so starch granules can be extracted.

quiz.q: How long does it take to manually grate 10 kg of cassava roots?
quiz.explanation: Manual grating is slow, taking about one hour for 10 kg.

quiz.q: What is a common power source for motorized graters in African small-scale processing?
options: B) 5-10 HP diesel engine or electric motor
quiz.explanation: Diesel engines or electric motors of 5-10 HP are commonly used.

quiz.q: Why should you add a little water during motorized grating?
options: A) To prevent overheating and help starch release
quiz.explanation: Water cools the grater and helps flush out starch granules.

quiz.q: What happens if the gap between the drum and casing of a motorized grater is too tight?
quiz.explanation: A too-tight gap causes the grater to jam and may damage the machine.

quiz.q: How often should you lubricate bearings and moving parts of a motorized grater?
quiz.explanation: Regular lubrication every 50 hours of use keeps the machine running smoothly.

quiz.q: What is a sign that grater teeth or blades need sharpening or replacement?
quiz.explanation: Dull teeth produce coarse pulp and reduce starch yield.

quiz.q: Why is it important to clean grating equipment immediately after use?
options: A) To prevent pulp from hardening and damaging teeth
quiz.explanation: Dried pulp can clog holes and break teeth, so immediate cleaning is essential.

quiz.q: What is a simple method to prevent rust on mild steel graters?
options: A) Coat with cooking oil after drying
quiz.explanation: A thin coat of cooking oil protects against rust.

quiz.q: How often should you change the oil in a diesel engine used for a grater?
quiz.explanation: Engine oil should be changed every 200 hours of operation.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for storing manual graters?
quiz.explanation: Hanging prevents contact with moisture and dirt, reducing rust.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a logbook for equipment maintenance?
options: A) To track usage and schedule maintenance
quiz.explanation: A logbook helps plan timely maintenance and avoid breakdowns.

quiz.q: What is the expected lifespan of a well-maintained motorized grater?
quiz.explanation: With proper care, a motorized grater can last 5-10 years.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a foreign material to remove from cassava roots?
quiz.explanation: Cassava starch is the desired product, not a foreign material.

quiz.q: What is the recommended maximum time between peeling and processing cassava roots?
quiz.explanation: Roots should be processed within 24 hours to avoid spoilage and browning.

quiz.q: Why is it important to use clean water for washing cassava roots?
options: A) To prevent contamination and off-flavours
quiz.explanation: Clean water prevents microbial contamination and ensures pure starch.

quiz.q: What is a simple hand-cranked peeler made from?
options: A) A metal drum with rough interior
quiz.explanation: A metal drum with rough interior can be used as a low-cost mechanical peeler.

quiz.q: What should you do if you suspect iron particles in cassava roots?
quiz.explanation: A magnet can attract and remove iron particles.
